newsitem.title: JORDAN: Iraq says technical issues hold up Jordan oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says technical issues hold up Jordan oil deal.

text.p: Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz said on Monday that "technical details" were holding up a deal under which Baghdad would supply Jordan with its entire oil needs for 1997.

Aziz told reporters that the terms of the deal, part of a wider protocol under which sanction-hit Baghdad supplies Amman with around 75,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and refined oil products in exchange for Jordanian goods, had yet to be resolved.
The accord is exempt from a strict United Nations trade embargo enforced on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
"We discussed the issues we need to take in the next few days to complete the economic accords between the two countries," Aziz told reporters after talks with Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.
"What are left are the technical details to conclude the accord and this is a matter in the hands of the Jordanian government," Aziz said without elaborating.

Few details or pricing mechanisms for the protocol, which is essentially a barter agreement, are published. Some of the oil is supplied free and another portion is given a nominal price at a discount to world market prices.

Jordan last year cut by half the value of goods it sent to Iraq to around $220 million, saying Baghdad's debts stood at around $1.2 billion and were increased by each annual protocol. It said the growing debts were draining its currency reserves.
Aziz questioned Jordan's claims of the debt, saying its imported goods were covered by the free oil.

"Due to sanctions, Iraq was buying goods and services from Jordan at the same value of the free oil," he said. "These were registered as debt, but Iraq has not borrowed money from Jordan...(it has) taken goods and services in return for this free oil it was granting," Aziz said.
Total Iraqi oil exports to Jordan are worth over $500 million a year at current market prices.
A top level meeting due on January 6 in Baghdad to seal the trade protocol was postponed after talks on the oil issue failed to reach agreement.

Iraq wants to cut the share of free oil to 45 percent from 50 percent and reduce the discount on the remaining oil, officials said. They said Iraq wanted more elbow room to buy more Jordanian goods under the trade protocol.
Jordan hopes it will persuade Iraq to keep the price unchanged at the preferrential rates despite steep rises in oil prices in the second half of 1996.
Jordanian officials said they did not believe Iraq's demand was political retaliation for King Hussein's distancing himself from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein since 1995.
Iraq had agreed to Jordan's request to raise the oil supplies in 1997 by seven percent to meet growth in local consumption, officials said.
Jordan has been trying to mend fences with Iraq since the announcement last month of the implementation of an Iraqi oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
